input: The purpose of this review is to examine in some detail the cost of a regional delivery route and to establish, as clearly as possible, what the route currently costs the business on an annual basis. Based on carrier invoices for the last 12 months, the route in question covers some 704 km per trip, at a cost of $1.74 per km, and operates 391 trips per year, which together give an annual transport cost of $479k. It should be noted that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the figure reflects the full cost of operating the route, including those legs on which the vehicle travels without a load. In other words, the $479k is not simply the cost of moving goods from one place to another; it is the cost of the entire pattern of movements that the route involves over the course of a year. This is an important consideration, because it means that the cost base already contains an element that is, at least in principle, open to challenge, namely the proportion of running that carries nothing at all. At the same time, it is worth bearing in mind that the invoices capture only what was actually paid during the period in question, and they do not, in themselves, say anything about what a differently organised route might cost, or about the level of service that customers on the route currently receive. Nevertheless, as a starting point for any further discussion, the review provides a single, clearly defined figure for the annual cost of the route as it is presently operated, together with the components from which that figure is built up, so that any proposed change can be assessed against a transparent and well-understood baseline.
target: Annual transport cost for the regional delivery route is $479k. The cost is computed from carrier invoices for the last 12 months. Each trip covers 704 km at $1.74 per km, and the route runs 391 trips per year. Empty running is included in the trip count. The annual figure is the price of every movement the route makes, loaded and empty together, at the invoiced rate. A trip that returns empty is not separated from a trip that returns loaded, and no part of the annual cost is assigned to the load alone. The invoice base fixes what the figure can support. Carrier invoices record what was paid for the work done, at the distances run and the rate charged. The $479k is a record of the present route, not an estimate of a redesigned one. A change in trip length, in the rate per kilometre, or in the number of trips changes the annual cost in proportion, and the review makes no claim about which of those changes is available. Empty running enters the cost through the trip count, and a reduction in empty running reduces the cost only where a trip is removed, not where a trip is merely better loaded. The figure carries no judgement about service. Delivery frequency, load size and arrival times stand outside the cost record, and a cheaper pattern of trips that failed the delivery requirement is not an improvement the invoices could show. What the review establishes is the cost of the route as run: the distance covered, the rate paid, and the trips made, over the months invoiced. Any proposal to change the route is measured against that base, component by component, and a saving claimed on one component is not netted against an increase in another without both being stated.
